title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 118: The Ancient Stepwells of Western India
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 118 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Ancient Stepwells of Western India

Paragraph 1. Across the dry plains of northwestern India, especially in Gujarat and Rajasthan, ancient builders created remarkable stone structures called stepwells. Known locally as baolis or vavs, these buildings are unique to the Indian subcontinent. Unlike ordinary vertical wells, where ropes and buckets pull water upward from the top, a stepwell is a deep multi-level stone trench. People walk down carved galleries below the ground to reach changing water levels.

Paragraph 2. Stepwells grew out of the extreme local climate. For nine months each year, northwestern India suffers intense heat and drought, followed by short monsoon rains lasting only a few weeks. Because the sandy soil absorbs rainwater very rapidly, surface streams dry up within days. To guarantee water during the dry season, early communities dug deep trenches into underground aquifers. When water levels fell in summer, villagers walked down long flights of stone steps to fill their pots.

Paragraph 3. Between the seventh and sixteenth centuries, stepwells changed from simple earth holes into grand stone monuments paid for by kings, wealthy merchants, and royal women. The finest surviving example is Rani ki Vav in Gujarat, ordered in 1063 CE by Queen Udayamati to honour her late husband, King Bhima I. Reaching over thirty metres underground across seven levels, Rani ki Vav features hundreds of decorated pillars and over eight hundred stone sculptures of gods and dancers.

Paragraph 4. Beyond supplying water, stepwells played an important social role. Because carrying household water was women's work, the shaded stone halls served as a daily gathering spot for village women to talk, share news, and perform religious ceremonies away from men. Moreover, deep stone walls and evaporating pool water acted like natural air conditioning. Temperatures inside were regularly six to ten degrees cooler than the hot air above, offering welcome rest to desert traders at midday.

Paragraph 5. Stepwells began to decline in the nineteenth century under British rule. Colonial officials thought the pools were unhealthy because villagers stepped straight into the standing water, spreading diseases like cholera. To stop infections, authorities installed iron hand-pumps and water pipes, filling many ancient stepwells with stones or blocking them with brick walls. Over time, unused channels filled with mud and rubbish. Recently, however, severe underground water shortages have led Indian conservationists to clear the mud and restore historic stepwells to collect seasonal rainwater once again.
